millimeter-wave systems have received little attention in the design of hybrid precoders. To fill this gap, we develop the first integrated design of analog transmit precoders and digital receive combiners for multicasting in mmWave systems, with each device having multiple phases and multiple antennas. By combining semidefinite relaxation, alternating optimization and Cholesky decomposition, we sequentially optimize the digital and analog components at the transmitter and receivers. The proposed method leads to significant performance improvements. Notably, with two receive antennas, we see an average reduction of $ 16.8\% $ in the transmit power needed per message and a rise of $ 60\% $ in the information successfully received. Simulation experiments demonstrate that the designed precoder system functions nearly as well as a fully-digital version even in the presence of difficult transmission conditions.

However, defining a utility function can be challenging in real-world problems due to the implicit and explicit nature of expert knowledge. To mitigate these issues, we've developed a utility function learning method that utilizes expert knowledge through preference learning, learned offline and incorporating coarse utility function information. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. driving and drone operation could benefit significantly from distributed machine learning (DML) over dynamically changing networks. Yet, standard weighted arithmetic mean aggregation in current DML systems may lead to considerable model inaccuracies and slow convergence speeds over fluctuating networks. In this paper, we introduce a new family of nonlinear aggregation functions to improve DML efficiency in networks subject to change. Our model utilizes a nonlinear weighted power mean aggregation approach rather than the linear aggregation typically employed by previous studies. By using mirror descent based on Bregman divergence for optimization and non-linear aggregation, we maintain the ability to agree on a single aggregation exponent for the entire network, thus simplifying the aggregation process. Our results demonstrate substantial model improvement and significant reduction in computation overhead compared to the existing linear aggregation method.

 Consequently, a higher level of complexity does not necessarily translate to a more reliable signature template, thereby challenging the conventional assumption in the field.

This investigation delves into the effects of heat on these high-order correlations as well.

The framework's source code has been made available on GitHub for public use.

undergone significant development and growth alongside the expansion of the internet. Since the launch of arXiv in 1991, preprints have increasingly shifted from physical to digital distribution. Preprints enable rapid and low-cost online dissemination of research findings to a broader audience within a matter of days. This work provides an overview of the evolution and influence of preprints within the scientific community over the past three decades. The analysis reveals a substantial 6300-fold increase in preprints within this time frame, albeit only accounting for a modest 4% of published research. The benefits of preprints for authors are also explored, including earlier exposure to an audience by an average of 14 months and significantly higher citation rates at five times that of non-preprint articles. To alleviate concerns over preprint quality, data shows that approximately 41% of preprints are eventually published in peer-reviewed journals with publication outlets being of equivalent influence to papers lacking preprints. The critical role of preprints in communicating emerging research during recent public health crises is also underscored. The quantitative findings presented aim to provide conclusive evidence of the positive impact of preprints on individual researchers and the broader scientific community, thus enhancing the efficiency of scholarly communication through accelerated and broadened dissemination of research findings facilitated by internet technologies.

The set of admissible entropies derived using the Ryu-Takayanagi formula corresponds to the Holographic Entropy Bondi-Wheeler-DeWitt theorem. This theorem describes the HAWK state's entropy across a splitting of the spacetime boundary into N regions, as being bounded by the HSW theorem. Although generating cell shapes randomly can help identify relevant genetic factors, overgeneralizing from random shapes to specific outcomes is not advisable.  Therefore, achieving cell shaping specificity required by living organisms poses a significant task.  We propose an innovative approach, inspired by the principle of kamytosis, to design a reward function that can optimize guide tube morphogenesis by focusing on distinct, achievement-oriented cell shape configurations.  We successfully derived a reward function from a simplified elliptical growth model that can be applied to any hyperelastic material.  We tested our proposed reward function in the context of both simple and complex tube geometries and found that it allowed for successful achievement of targeted cell shape configurations that cannot be reached using traditional gradient-based methods.  We found that optimizing the proposed reward function was robust to variations in the viscoelastic growth model and the viscous dissipation parameter.  This research demonstrates a framework for defining actionable, achievement-oriented rewards for autonomous morphogenesis, which may be applied to other cell shape optimization tasks.

By dividing the disk arrangement into segments and constructing species of particles with statistically interacting behaviors, exact calculations for jammed configurations are obtained, allowing for a detailed understanding of volume and entropy. It is discovered that jammed configurations can be categorized based on the movement patterns of particles and segments, and the resulting entropies are found to depend on this classification. Additionally, the observed statistical invariance to disk orientation leads to a natural splitting of the disk population into two distinct groups, where the large disks exhibit independent movement patterns, resulting in an associated entropy contribution. This distinction enables a Jammed Configurational Entropy (JCE) approximation, which can accurately represent the overall disk population's statistical behavior. The JCE approximation is found to converge towards the overall jammed configurational energy as the disk size difference increases, and the accuracy of this approximation is validated through various numerical analyses.

star mergers in numerical relativity are conducted to obtain a comprehensive picture of the inspiral, merger, and post-merger stages.  The analysis across various initial and computational configurations reveals universally similar evolution processes, regardless of setup variations.  The disruption of the neutron star leads to the formation of a massive quark star or a strange star, accompanied by the creation of a massive jet that emerges from the equatorial plane and is powered by the neutron star's angular momentum.  The initial break-up of the neutron star takes approximately 20-30 milliseconds, resulting in the formation of a massive quark star or strange star, with the quark star weighing up to 2.2 solar masses and exhibiting a radius of approximately 10 kilometers.  The energetic event emission is attributed to the neutron star's exterior layers being ejected during the merger and the formation of a massive quark star or strange star, with properties similar to those observed in gamma-ray bursts.  The massive quark star or strange star may experience a second birth, resulting from the neutron star's core collapsing into a quark star or strange star, or may instead be covered by a tidal disk and become a quark or strange star with an irregular surface.

is a long-established concern in manufacturing when multiple robots are involved. Although single robot scheduling has been extensively researched, the problem becomes more complex when multiple robots need to be scheduled, requiring shared access to workpieces and tools. To address this challenge, a new heuristic known as the Modified Optical Recognition (MOR) has been developed. MOR integrates a robot task allocation phase and a scheduling phase. In the task allocation phase, MOR employs a modified dominos recognition to simultaneously assign tools and schedule tasks efficiently. In the scheduling phase, MOR applies the Modified Insertion Time (MIT) to generate an initial schedule, which is subsequently improved using a greedy improvement algorithm to produce a high-quality schedule with minimal tool changes and reduced waiting times. Compared to current methods, MOR has shown superior performance on large industrial datasets. Notably, when a single robot is used, MOR's average deviation from the optimal schedule is 2.71%. When multiple robots are involved, MOR's average deviation from the optimal schedule is 4.39%.

This study addresses the query of whether randomizing the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer, using protocols like frequency-hopping multiple access and ALOHA, can mitigate the adverse effects of interference correlation. semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using the same loss function, failing to acknowledge their distinct contributions to classification. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on labeling nodes with the greatest informative value, which effectively represents local neighborhoods through mutual information maximization. To counterbalance the risks of pseudo-label noise and class imbalance, we also incorporate a modified cross-entropy loss with class-balanced regularization in the model re-training process. Comprehensive experiments on six graph datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, which outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised graph classification methods.

implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. Consequently, a generalized global pooling layer for neural networks called UOT-Pooling (UOTP) has been proposed. To implement this UOTP layer, the classic Sinkhorn-scaling algorithm is employed. Furthermore, a new model architecture based on the Bregman ADMM algorithm is designed, which offers better numerical stability and improved ability to reproduce existing pooling layers. The proposed UOTP layers are then tested across several applications, including multi-instance learning, graph classification, and image classification, and are found to be capable of either mimicking conventional global pooling layers or developing novel, performance-enhancing pooling mechanisms.

From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model prior to execution, whereas MitM attacks can launch without this limitation. Our results show that our approach enables successful MitM attacks on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, outperforming existing attack techniques. Moreover, our research reveals that a VAE-based system can function as a generative adversarial network, yielding comparable performance to existing GAN designs, such as BigGAN.

In this research, two methods that determine the spin of a black hole from an accretion disk signal in gravitational waves are explored. ersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces an innovative solution based on a long short-term memory (LSTM) model for channel estimation. The proposed method incorporates an LSTM unit for channel estimation, followed by a temporal averaging technique to mitigate noise, and analytically calculates the noise mitigation ratio to verify its effectiveness. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution surpasses the performance of recently proposed DL-based estimators, while also achieving substantial reductions in computational complexity.

Increasing the MLRP's memory requirements further amplifies the need for a large and complex generative model. In this paper, we present an efficient way to use standard generative models that don't need a big MLRP on a large dataset of pixels. MA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements for CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 revealed a significantly higher mass range ($0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$) than those typically obtained from binary formation simulations, which were around $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$. In response to these disparities, researchers carried out numerical simulations of a core's collapse to analyze how a binary system's formation mass is influenced by the core's initial instability parameter and radial wobble during the core collapse process. Their model considered two types of binary formation:'mergers' that result from radial wobble and 'fragments' formed through Kelvin-Helmholz instabilities at the core's edge. Preliminary results from these simulations demonstrate that a binary system's mass is largely determined by the core's initial instability parameter in'merger' scenarios, while in 'fragments' scenarios, the binary system's mass is largely influenced by the radial wobble during the core collapse process. Therefore, researchers can adjust the initial conditions in 'fragments' scenarios to match observed proto-stellar masses measured in binary systems.

This occurs under specific conditions where the interactions between particles cause the lowest single-particle states to be filled and the highest states to be empty. In the exciton condensation phenomenon, the inverse occurs, with the lowest single-particle states being occupied and the highest single-polariton states being empty. general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to pairs of $n$-dimensional vectors, $g \otimes_f h$ is calculated as the sum of the products of the function values of $g$ and $h$ for each possible pair. This framework encompasses multiple known convolutions, including the Modulo Convolution and the Complex Convolution. A modulo convolution is obtained by using the element-wise modulo operation, while a complex convolution is derived by using the standard Cartesian product of $D$. A key finding in this research is the presentation of a new complex convolution that is neither a modulo convolution nor equivalent to another existing complex convolution. Additionally, this study confirms that the four-dimensional complex convolution over a specific domain $D=\{0,1\}$ is distinct from its modulo counterpart.

we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole in a canonical ensemble as stipulated by the weak gravity conjecture, the perturbation must breach the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to compute higher-order corrections to black holes in anti-de Sitter space and to Kerr black holes.

requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
To address this, we introduce the MemoNav network, which employs a self-adapting memory mechanism to optimize the fraction of relevant information in its memory.
The MemoNav network consists of a visual navigation agent, a self-adapting memory mechanism, and a multi-task training method that includes both navigation and visual recognition tasks.
Through multi-task training, the network learns to optimize the fraction of relevant information in its memory, allowing it to better perform navigation tasks and automatically adapt to various environments, eliminating the need for manual tuning.

a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. The paper provides information about the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The investigation of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state, rather than through the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state, can be performed through an advanced analysis of the energy distribution of the three $\alpha$ particles from the decay. Using beta-delayed charged-particle spectroscopy on $^{12}\mathrm{N}$, an excited 0+ state at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$ is examined to investigate the non-sequential behavior of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay. The analysis shows a significant component of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay, with a lower limit of 35% compared to sequential processes. The measurement of the trimeric decay width of the Hoyle state is also obtained, with a calculated width of 2.1 keV for the three $\alpha$ particles having the same momentum as expected from a calculable width in the three-body decay system.

Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. Through phase-field fracture models, we find the following features of this oscillatory instability: (i) It also exists in materials with linear elastic behavior near the crack, depending solely on dissipation properties; (ii) It undergoes a type of supercritical bifurcation; and (iii) It's minimally affected by factors like the fracture energy associated with a certain dissipation time. These results support the idea that this oscillatory instability is an inherent feature of fast cracks in 2D, while we also show that an ultra-high speed instability can be attributed to a limiting rate of energy transport near the crack. The numerical framework of the fracture approach used in this study is thoroughly described.

AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by using more advanced symbolic surrogate models but, since these typically demand symbolic inputs not commonly available in computer vision, we instead explore a new method: Utilizing intrinsic network features, we create a comprehensive 3D Rubik's Cube representation of any deep neural network's behavior using its intrinsic features as variables. This unique visualization enables in-depth analysis of model performance and allows for the incorporation of human expertise. Due to computational demands, we optimize the method for efficient training and demonstrate its success on multiple complex vision tasks, including the analysis of medical diagnosis models and exposure of AI biases.

graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy.

Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing range of both a credible second-price auction and a first-price auction. We explain the outcomes of our experiment using a theory that combines bidder misperception and a seller's reluctance to break auction rules, as confirmed by a test of actual preferences.

Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This insight enables the precise manipulation of heat within microscopic devices through phase-coherence. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling system was used to demonstrate that interference affects the charge current, but its influence is most pronounced on thermal current. This discovery leads to the prediction that heat rectification capabilities could be enhanced by adjusting an external magnetic field. By fine-tuning the magnetic field, the system can transition through multiple heat rectification modes or shift towards a regime with minimal thermal current. Notably, our findings are substantiated by detailed numerical results, which confirm their applicability to other systems exhibiting edge states driven by phase-coherent quantum interference.

SARS-CoV-2 in 2020, was officially classified as a global health crisis by the WHO. This research aims to address these concerns by presenting the successful implementation of a public-facing data platform as a model solution to the existing data-related problems.

Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the black holes' low mass. The radiation's intensity and spectrum are characterized by a lack of significant features at high frequencies, which contradicts the findings of recent studies. rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation speed compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. KIC 9267654's behavior differs significantly from that of higher mass giants, which often exhibit slower outer layers and faster inner cores due to a faster core rotation speed. This unique rotation profile for KIC 9267654 might be the result of a massive early planetary object that has migrated inward and become trapped at a location near the 0.03 RJ core radius, causing desynchronization between core and outer layer rotation speeds.

Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems like LIN and CONST-DELAY-lin, an enumeration class of problems that can be computed after linear-time preprocessing. The proposed computation model has limited storage and processing capabilities - its registers can store $O(N)$ elements, where $N$ is the input size, and perform basic arithmetic operations on them. Specifically, it shows that LIN is a proper subset of the family of problems computed by the new RAM model and that this model is robust under various transformations, including changes in the initial input size or computation time. The study also establishes that even slight changes in the computation model result in significant algorithmic differences.

Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained using standard knowledge distillation techniques. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms, including the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains significant mass per unit time, exceeding a certain threshold. Conversely, weakly magnetized clouds produce high-speed jets consistently across a wide range of mass accumulation rates. The reason for this discrepancy lies in the way magnetic field is accumulated and amplified in the protostar's surrounding environment. In weakly magnetized clouds, the ambient angular momentum is easily exchanged, allowing the protostar to remove excess angular momentum and produce high-speed jets, regardless of the mass accumulation rate. In strongly magnetized clouds, the ambient angular momentum is poorly exchanged, resulting in poor jet production unless the protostar accumulates mass at a high rate, causing the magnetic field to wind up rapidly and produce the characteristic two-phase jet structure.

This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points, a generalised equality relation applicable to quantities differing by negligible terms, and a continuity principle stating that a quantity can be equal to another quantity that is itself continuous.

The analysis involves determining the impact of removing foregrounds and beam effects on the estimation of parameters, and how this varies with the degree of beam correction. The removal of foregrounds significantly affects the accuracy of parameter estimation, with an optimal beam width for foreground removal that allows further reduction in errors on parameters being identified. The errors on parameters are reduced when accounting for the uncertainty in the foreground removal process, and the errors are as expected following the law of error propagation for a function. The errors on parameters are reduced if the experiment were to be like PUMA rather than CHORD or a stage IV galaxy survey.

focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in G's actions on spaces. We explore growth related to actions on simplicial complexes, particularly when the degree of each vertex is bounded. We find that a group G exhibits bounded growth within an associated space if and only if G has a torsion-free subgroup with bounded growth. This growth condition is equivalent to a group having polynomial growth of a specific degree. We establish a connection between growth in groups G and the properties of associated transformation semigroups. We show that a group G has subexponential growth if and only if the transformation semigroup induced by G on an associated space has a bounded number of images per state. We establish the bounded growth property in certain groups, such as torsion-free horospherical spaces and arithmetic lattice groups. We demonstrate that a solvable group G exhibits exponential growth if it has a torsion-free abelian normal subgroup. We prove that a group G has subexponential growth if it has a torsion-free subgroup with subexponential growth. We introduce the concept of mean growth, a measure of growth within a group that is more sensitive to certain subgroups than the group itself. We show that a group G has mean growth of type $\alpha$ if and only if a related transformation semigroup has a specific property related to its type $\alpha$ growth rate. We establish the mean growth type for certain groups, such as the groups corresponding to number fields and their associated properties.

The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. A second, more advanced detector is also presented which utilizes a deeper analysis of the movement of biological species by breaking down their movement into different components. This second detector is created by training neural network indicators with a wealth of simulated data, produced using a tool that allows for the controlled creation of movement scenarios, ranging from simple to complex. The effectiveness of the detection methods is tested on a variety of real-world videos showing the movement of different species, with the results showing that the second detector is capable of accurately identifying the movement of biological species in most cases.

(ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. Primarily, such methods must be able to effectively account for the inherent discrepancies between theoretical models and measurements by introducing corresponding discrepancy models into their formulations. Secondly, these methods should ensure that the proposed universal physical laws are free from contradictions that could arise from the consideration of additional factors. Lastly, these methods should be capable of providing a thorough understanding of all assumptions that are fundamental to the discovery process, without which universal laws that are derived from the measurements can be seen as meaningless. By addressing these challenges, several alternative data-driven approaches to classic methods of physics discovery are presented in this work. These approaches not only provide a more complete understanding of the object's motion but also clarify the role of gravity in the universal law that describes the motion of objects at various scales.

Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. To explain this phenomenon, we investigated the stability of these space transformations. This paper demonstrates that any cloud having a stabilizer with nontrivial action will contain a unique central metric space, such that transformations from the stabilizer all converge to this space, thereby indicating that it is zero distance away from all others within that group. The key proof for this lies within our previously published paper, while the main focus here is the understanding and description of this central metric space.

Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, but in the inverse direction. In contrast to the widely accepted intuition, this scale does not coincide with the dissipation length. In general, fluctuation effects are only substantial when the Strouhal number based on this scale is not sufficiently large. In specific situations where the energy-containing scale is the predominant feature, this Strouhal number can be too small. In particular, this is evident in the case of Taylor--Reynolds fluctuations at low Reynolds numbers, in wakes at low wave numbers, in channel flow at specific locations, and in the case of very weak nonlinearity in three-dimensional turbulence with Reynolds numbers independent of the Taylor microscale. In all these instances, the Kolmogorov microscale is significantly larger than the relevant length scale, implying that the Reynolds number based on this scale is too low for the fluctuation effect to materialize. In contrast, this effect may potentially be measurable in three-dimensional turbulence with high Reynolds numbers not dependent on the Taylor microscale.

The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new approach for computing the Shapley value for training examples within a holistic machine learning pipeline is proposed. The approach establishes a connection between the Shapley value and equilibria in strategic games, allows for a generalisation of the Laplace mechanism, and provides a novel understanding of data privacy by relating the Shapley value to the privacy budget. The approach's efficacy is demonstrated through numerical experiments conducted on a dataset of Amazon Amazonia documents.

One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, toppling robots, and costly damages when physical harm occurs.
To overcome this issue, we've developed a fully immersive virtual reality environment that puts a robot in a 3D room filled with obstacles and challenges for a human operator to overcome by issuing verbal commands to navigate, explore, and solve complex problems to progress.
Our system transports the user into a VR world, mimicking the robot's visual perspective and sensing capabilities, making remote operation a seamless experience.
To test the effectiveness of our system, we've set up a study where humans operated the robot remotely in a challenging mission, first using our new VR environment and then in a similar physical setup.
The results showed that performance differences between remote and physical settings were minimal, and crucially, our study found that incorporating a VR immersive experience led to significantly better operational performance compared to a less engaging non-immersive setup.
Consequently, we've set up a public challenge that pits text-based virtual agents against each other in this novel VR scenario, aiming to spur innovation in both automated agent development and more effective human-agent collaboration.

Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing a matrix factorization framework with sparsity and low-rank constraints to integrate local and global structures. Through the propagation of this low-rank structure, our method achieves significantly improved sparsity for representing the original Gabor filter bank. Our experimental results show that OCNs outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and computational cost, with a significant reduction in model complexity.

This difficulty arises from not only the typical problems of sample size and model complexity but also the unique challenges posed by overfitting to sparse data and the propagation of uncertainties from input data. By contrasting the magnetic properties of MnSe$_2$ and FeSe$_2$, the research revealed distinct features and characteristics, with MnSe$_2$ exhibiting a more complex magnetic structure due to magnetic interaction than FeSe$_2$. This gives rise to a frequency spectrum, denoted by $A(k,t)$, which counts the number of family groups of size $k$ in the population at time $t$. The frequency spectrum process represents a type of non-Markovian branching process belonging to a class of random-characterized branching processes. This work aims to propose approximation methods that enable $A(k,t)$ to be approximated by a continuous function when $t$ is sufficiently large and the mutation rate is relatively small. The primary goal is to establish a central limit theorem for $A(k,t)$, tail probability bounds for extreme family groups, and an upper bound for a rare family group. This enables such rare family groups to be eliminated in the population, resulting in a simplified model. A continuous function can then be used to approximate the simplified model, thereby effectively eliminating these groups. The validity of this new approximation is guaranteed by a confidence interval for extreme family groups, thereby ensuring that this new approximation does not significantly distort the overall population distribution. advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. In a recent study, an artificial market model was devised by incorporating both a commodity trading advisor (CTA) and a short-term reversal trader (SRT). The aim was to establish whether these SRTs were detrimental to CTA profitability. Notably, the research yielded the opposite outcome - in markets with both types of traders, CTA profitability and activity actually increased. Consequently, a positive symbiotic relationship between these traders may exist, challenging the widely-held assumption that SRTs undermine CTAs.

Although pinpointing the application protocol can be challenging, solely relying on static characteristics like port numbers can be insufficient. As a result, advanced and adaptive approaches have been developed for more precise identification. In this research, the mechanisms of several prominent attack detection systems are examined to understand how they pinpoint the application protocol. Our analysis reveals that these systems primarily utilize predictive indicators, including data format, while also considering other features. In an effort to enhance the systems, our approach utilizes machine learning, specifically a neural network, to teach a system capable of protocol identification using network traffic data. Our approach is empirical in nature and relies on real-world network traffic, as well as a comparison with the systems of leading network security providers, to pinpoint the application protocol in Google's public data set. Our results indicate that our approach is capable of significantly decreasing the system's overhead, as compared to the adaptive and fixed approaches, while maintaining an exceptional accuracy rate of 97.22%.

urIPS 2021 - AWS Deepracer challenge, which required developing a self-driving vehicle model that interacts with its environment through action-reward interactions. The goal was to create a model that could navigate a track, adapt to real-world physics, and optimize performance via reinforcement learning. To overcome this limitation, we combined multiple models in an ensemble to mitigate overfitting, and then employed transfer learning with a pre-trained model that had been trained on a similar dataset called Torus-Gridworld. The model was then evaluated on a validation set and optimized for maximum performance before being submitted for evaluation, where it consistently ranked near the top of all submitted models, with a combined track completion score of 94.7%.

2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and the outcome of the competition revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced scenario.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text models capable of providing more reliable and robust predictions.

Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. This workload can be significantly alleviated when the models are deployed on specialized Hardware Accelerators, but only if the accelerated models exhibit comparable performance to the original. This paper presents a novel and efficient method for constraining small CNN model size while maintaining high accuracy. Our approach leverages the structural similarities between standard 3x3 CNN filters and the elements of the Hermite Matrix, enabling a direct connection between them. This allows us to interpret certain CNN filters as generalized radial basis function interpolation nodes and to develop an efficient method for reducing their size. Our core contribution is a novel radial bias learning strategy that maintains the stationarity of the CNN filters while minimizing their size. This involves adding a balancing term to the stationarity loss function and selecting optimal radial bias values. Our experiments show that our approach decreases the size of the CNN filters, resulting in a 50% reduction in the memory requirements and inference time, while maintaining an accuracy loss of less than 2%. This makes our method suitable for deployment on small Hardware Accelerators, such as the NMSU Beaver, with the same level of performance as larger models twice its size.

giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star called TOI-5542 approximately every 75 days. Initially detected by the TESS satellite, the exoplanet, which has a radius similar to that of Jupiter, has been further confirmed using data from ground-based spectrographic equipment. Two approaches are commonly used to resolve issues of constraint violations in CMDPs: the constrained dynamic programming method, which directly handles constraints, and the gradient projection method, which involves relaxing the constraints and minimizing a penalty term. The gradient projection method is commonly associated with the policy iteration algorithm. Although gradient projection is typically subject to convergence issues, research has shown that under specific conditions, convergence is ensured and a constrained optimal policy can be achieved. The optimal constrained policy can also be obtained by using the exponentiated gradient projection algorithm, a deterministic algorithm independent of variables. We present a new variant of the exponentiated gradient projection algorithm, ensuring convergence even at a slower rate. Theoretical convergence analysis and empirical performance validation through simulations in real-life settings and a job scheduling problem are presented.

Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-action data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness significantly depends on this parameter's proper choice. Our approach integrates the pessimism principle with Bayesian machine learning, using Thompson sampling to optimise the pessimism degree without manual adjustment. By developing a credible set with an optimistically bounded Q-function boundary, the need for a pessimism parameter disappears. Our general Bayesian learning method is applicable to a range of models, including a Bayesian policy neural network. The benefits of our approach are particularly evident in simple Bayesian models, which often have an analytically determinable state transition model, allowing for the implementation of a more effective pessimism principle. Our theoretical analysis, along with extensive empirical tests, demonstrate the value of our approach.

, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. Researchers can utilize this modified XANES technique to assess timescales ranging from a few femtoseconds to a few picoseconds, thereby gaining insight into how electronic excitations and their recombination progress affect a material's density and molecular structure. The technique has been applied to two materials - amorphous germanium and a geothermal germanium oxide - to investigate the effects of their initial density on density changes due to intense X-ray radiation and demonstrate that small variations in molecular structure across amorphous geeks can lead to noticeably different behavioral responses. The research has paved the path for using advanced X-ray techniques to differentiate various materials and varied environmental conditions, thus bringing us closer to understanding potential practical applications and left unanswered questions regarding the unique properties of XANES at the sub-picosecond timescale.

The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics.

we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources attributed to neutron star mergers. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency radiation at 41 kHz, stemming from mass fluctuations near the point of closest approach, and later transitions to higher-energy signals at 6.3 E52 ergs, characterized by tidal instability, and ultimately stabilizes into lower-energy bursts. In our analysis, we explore the spectrum of electromagnetic waves emitted and the resultant effects on observable X-ray signals, incorporating factors of quantum pressure and electromagnetic forces. Our research aims to initiate an in-depth examination of the accretion process and its electromagnetic implications.

bukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than $0$. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function, denoted as $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, represents a semimetric for all possible subsets of a given set. Our research found that the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is indeed a metric if $\alpha$ lies within the interval from $0$ to $0.5$ and $\beta$ is greater than or equal to $1/(1-\alpha)$. The special case where $\alpha$ equals $0.5$ results in the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ simplifying to the well-known Jaccard distance.

However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmentation technique to create blurry inputs dynamically during training and testing. To make the most of this approach, we adopt an unconventional framework incorporating a sequential process of blur removal and image reconstruction instead of a traditional end-to-end approach. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by presenting an improved model that surpasses state-of-the-art deblurring methods, achieving the best results on various challenging real-world blurry images and videos.

To explore the properties of the resulting series, Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 was studied via HAXPES. Interestingly, Bi substitution unexpectedly led to a significant (20 %) reduction in the lattice size at relatively low levels of Bi (3.5 %) doping. English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data labeling, development time, and expertise. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and discovered that it surpasses the performance of numerous strong baselines while matching or even exceeding state-of-the-art results obtained through more resource-intensive and complicated methods. Moreover, our framework successfully captures rich, semantically significant representations across languages despite the absence of direct supervision.

monitoring the atmosphere's flow patterns and snowflake trajectories in real time. A state-of-the-art, high-resolution imaging system is utilized to capture snowflakes in motion, mapping the flow patterns and detecting vortex formations above the ground. Concurrently, a high-resolution camera is employed to track individual snowflakes in a smaller sample area within the main field of view, revealing the connection between atmospheric turbulence and snowflake settling patterns. Our research reveals that as snowflakes interact with turbulence at critical velocities, their falling speed is greatly increased, a phenomenon not seen in prior studies. Images captured within the flow patterns show that snowflakes tend to concentrate near the base of vortex formations, moving preferentially downwards. High-resolution footage of these vortex formations provides quantitative evidence of accelerated snowflake speeds. This study provides comprehensive evidence that a phenomenon called preferential sweeping is the primary cause of enhanced snow deposition in the atmosphere's lower layers.

how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that the mental framework created through learning can be utilized in accordance with the principles of active inference, enabling seamless integration within the overall theoretical framework. This research marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning to real-world, high-dimensional sensory data, paving the way for innovative applications in cognitive neuroscience and related fields.

Real-life occurrences typically involve connected entities and thus can be represented as clusters in network data. Yet, current learning approaches struggle to recognize event-based data, even when cluster information is available.  To address this shortcoming, we propose an event evaluation framework that assesses the relevance of learning models by analyzing their ability to identify occurrences and their duration. This framework is versatile and adaptable to various forms of network data, including networks, link, and attribute-based datasets.  To further enhance the understanding of event-based learning, we studied the characteristics of successful benchmark models and discovered that our proposed framework produces comparable results with these benchmarks.  This study investigates the efficacy of our event-based evaluation framework and explores the requirements for learning models to be effective in this domain.

our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence depends on the minimum entropy associated with the corresponding node in the confusion graph, known as the transmission entropy. Our study establishes various metrics to measure the adversary's information gain and reveals their interconnected relationships. Furthermore, these metrics are applied to explore how multiple adversaries with distinct objectives interact with each other.

A new hierarchical generative model called MrSARP is introduced in this research, specifically designed for Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) image generation based on scene characteristics like size and shape. We investigated magnetic excitations of the Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with longer-range hopping. Beginning with a magnetic order that doesn't appear in pure quantum models, we discovered two types of magnetic excitations - one stable and the other leading to instability. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, vertebrae center activation maps are generated, which are then adjusted along the spine's central axis to produce optimized activation maps that can be aggregated into 1-dimensional activation signals. Building upon this, an anatomically-constrained optimization module is integrated to jointly determine the optimal positions of the vertebrae. The optimization is performed under a flexible constraint that ensures the distance between vertebrae and a rigid constraint that maintains consecutive vertebrae indices. Upon being evaluated using a well-established public dataset consisting of 302 CT images characterized by significant spinal pathologies, the proposed method achieved the highest identification rate of 97.4% and surpassed the best comparable approach, which reported an identification rate of 94.7%, by significantly reducing the relative error rate.

The flow rates of physical processes are calculated from the anti-symmetric transition measures defined on the network of states. The statistical behavior of these flow rates can be represented by normalized cumulants. This study applies the mathematical and topological structure of Markovian models to demonstrate the gauge invariance of the normalized cumulant-generating function. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." This perspective of Galileo's lack of mathematical skills has significant implications for evaluating his scientific legacy.

A key characteristic of Tsallis statistics is the non-zero value of the ground state entropy. This property is explored in detail in the present work. A systematic analysis of the ground state entropy is conducted using three distinct methods: mathematical algebra, specialization of physical systems, and a generalized hydrodynamic approach. These analyses reveal the necessity of a constant term in the ground state entropy expression, which is a fundamental feature of Tsallis' thermodynamic framework. A concrete example is presented to illustrate the validity of the Constant Term Hypothesis. Furthermore, the study outlines a generalized hydrodynamic approach that can be utilized to determine the temperature dependence of thermodynamic properties from experimental data measured at various temperatures. This approach is particularly useful in describing behavior in both the thermodynamic and pretmodynamic regimes.

Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enhances computational efficiency. The results indicate that the MHD-AEPIC model accurately replicates key aspects of the two MHD scenarios with embedded PIC models, showing comparable reconnection rates and rope alignment. The MHD-AEPIC model exhibits minor discrepancies in magnetic field and particle numbers, manageable for practical applications, and displays computational efficiency gains of up to two orders of magnitude compared to traditional MHD simulations with embedded PIC models.
